title: Microsoft and Opella Build Lumen to Verify AI Health Content at Scale
excerpt: The agentic platform uses 14 specialized agents to check product claims, medical facts and legal mentions across Opella's 21,000 AI-generated assets, with human experts keeping final approval.
body:
• Microsoft and Opella are building Lumen, an agentic AI platform with 14 specialized agents that check health content for product claims, medical facts, sources and legal mentions.
  • Opella has scaled AI content production 30-fold to more than 21,000 assets with 85 people across six content factories, making human review the bottleneck Lumen targets.
  • Medical, legal and regulatory experts keep the final decision on every asset under Opella's principle: "Human first. Human last."
  • Opella is Sanofi's former consumer healthcare business, independent since 2025, with 100 brands including Allegra, Dulcolax and Enterogermina.

Microsoft and consumer healthcare company Opella are partnering to build Lumen, an agentic artificial intelligence platform designed to verify health content at scale, the companies announced on October 20, 2026. Lumen uses 14 specialized AI agents to check each piece of content for product claims, medical facts, sources and legal mentions, and to advise where content should be placed by type and publication channel, according to Opella's announcement. The agents flag what is compliant, what needs correcting and what requires human judgment, and explain every recommendation.

Why Opella needs verification at scale

Opella created the problem Lumen is meant to solve. Its in-house generative AI content engine, called Wonka internally, grew from a small Paris team to six factories worldwide with more than 85 people and more than 21,000 AI-generated assets available to marketers, with engagement up around 50%. Content output grew 30-fold, and Opella says compliance checks became the bottleneck. The company estimates that around 100 million pieces of health content enter the digital ecosystem every day and that at least half is incomplete, misleading or wrong. MobiHealthNews reported the same structure: the proof of concept's 14 agents flag medical facts, product claims, scientific references, legal requirements and local market and channel rules, then direct reviewers to the areas needing closer attention.

"But in healthcare, speed can never come at the expense of trust. That's why, with Lumen, we're using AI to help our experts review content faster and make better-informed decisions, while keeping human expertise and approval at the heart of the process."

— Alberto Hernandez, Chief Growth Officer, Opella

How the human check stays in charge

Both companies stress that Lumen does not approve content. Medical, legal and regulatory experts retain responsibility for final decisions, a model Opella summarises as "Human first. Human last." Fierce Healthcare reported that Lumen will flag compliance issues and corrections and identify where human input is needed, emphasising that human experts keep the final decision. The design mirrors a wider pattern in regulated industries: agents handle volume and consistency checks, while accountable specialists sign off, because a wrong dosage claim or an unsubstantiated product claim carries regulatory consequences that a general marketing error does not.

Opella and Microsoft in context

Opella is the world's third-largest player in over-the-counter medicines and vitamins, minerals and supplements, reaching around half a billion consumers. Headquartered in France, it has 11,000 employees, 13 manufacturing sites and 100 brands, including Allegra, Buscopan, Doliprane, Dulcolax, Enterogermina, Essentiale and Mucosolvan. The business was Sanofi's consumer healthcare arm until it launched as an independent company in 2025, and it is a certified B Corporation. For Microsoft, Lumen adds to a run of healthcare AI work that Fierce Healthcare catalogued: a strategic collaboration with Mayo Clinic announced in June to build a frontier AI model for healthcare, planned for release through Azure Foundry APIs, and Copilot Health for consumers, unveiled in March.

What to watch

Lumen is starting as a proof of concept inside Opella's own content operation, not a product other companies can buy today. The test that matters is measurable: whether 14 checking agents cut review time on 21,000-plus assets without letting claim or reference errors through, and whether regulators accept an agent-assisted review trail with a named human approver. If it works at Opella's scale, the same pattern, specialised verification agents under human sign-off, is the template other consumer health and pharmaceutical marketers will be pressed to adopt as AI content volumes keep rising.
